deal_summary: The buyer considered an available machine after a prior supplier dispute and pursued leasing. The offer moved through product specification, a tripartite contract and legal review, then a signed contract and leasing payment. The final events show a sharp readiness/logistics mismatch: funds reached the seller while the customer's driver was already waiting and the machine still needed work. The seller had not confirmed same-day readiness. [evidence: 1, 2, 3, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 18]

customer_need.summary: An in-stock labeling machine for round packaging with a capper, delivered through Baltic Leasing; the parties later needed to specify two container sizes, label details, and the final equipment name. Initial availability and the 3M price threshold are stated in a manager worklog, not directly confirmed by the buyer in the call excerpt. [evidence: 0, 1, 4, 7]

deal_dynamics.early: The buyer said a previous supplier relationship had broken down and expected to proceed after internal review; the leasing route and direct manager contact were discussed. [evidence: 1]
deal_dynamics.middle: Progress depended on collecting exact product dimensions and settling whether the sale contract would be bilateral or tripartite, how warranty obligations would be recorded, and what documentation leasing required. Product naming changed during revisions, prompting another confirmation. [evidence: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
deal_dynamics.late: A tripartite agreement was signed and returned as a scan. Leasing then sought equipment photos/video before paying, while the seller said customization and final assembly depended on payment. After funds arrived, the buyer's driver was waiting, but the equipment was not ready for immediate loading. [evidence: 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 18]

positive_signals: Buyer described an active purchase need after the earlier supplier arrangement failed and expected internal review to finish soon. [evidence: 1]
Buyer had already sent product dimensions to another contact and later pursued an urgent delivery date. [evidence: 2, 14]
Buyer-side contact asked about obtaining the equipment by Wednesday, arranged a driver, and offered to complete a small assembly task with its own technicians. [evidence: 14, 18]
negative_signals: The buyer-side contact said she had no time to complete a specification form and believed the exact dimensions had already been supplied. [evidence: 2]
The buyer's driver arrived before seller readiness had been confirmed, creating immediate pressure and frustration. [evidence: 14, 18]
customer_behavior.initiative: Buyer-side staff supplied or routed dimensions, coordinated lease approval, requested shipment timing, and tried to solve the late assembly delay by offering its own technical staff. [evidence: 1, 2, 14, 18]
customer_behavior.decision_process: The purchase involved the lessee, Baltic Leasing, and the seller. Leasing legal review determined contract structure and warranty wording; the buyer's payment to the lessor was followed by payment from leasing to the seller. [evidence: 3, 7, 9, 11, 12]

strong_actions: Stayed in contact with the customer and leasing representatives and obtained product dimensions from the buyer-side contact's colleague when she could not complete a form. [evidence: 1, 2, 4]
Worked through tripartite contract and warranty requirements with the lessor, and supplied requested compliance documentation. [evidence: 3, 5, 6, 8, 9]
Asked leasing whether a separate invoice was needed and investigated delivery/acceptance alternatives. [evidence: 11, 14, 15, 16]
weak_actions: The final equipment name changed multiple times, and leasing explicitly asked the seller to confirm one final name for the lease documents. [evidence: 7]

The payment/inspection dependency was not resolved before signature: leasing required photos/video to release funds, while the seller said final assembly and client-specific labeling required those funds. [evidence: 11, 12]
The manager could not give the waiting driver a firm shipment time after payment arrived; coordination of readiness, loading and transport was still open. [evidence: 14, 15, 16, 18]
manager_behavior.follow_up_quality: Responsive across a complex three-party documentation chain, but operational updates became reactive at the payment and shipment stage; the buyer asked repeatedly for timing and a callback. [evidence: 3, 5, 7, 9, 14, 15, 18]
manager_behavior.next_step_control: Contract and documentation steps were eventually completed, but the view ends with no agreed loading time or delivery plan after funds arrived. The manager promised to check with production and call back. [evidence: 9, 10, 14, 15, 16, 18]

turning_points.description: The buyer explained that an earlier supplier arrangement had broken down and expected the current purchase to proceed after review. [evidence: 1]
The seller's contract specialist and lessor debated bilateral versus tripartite terms and warranty coverage; they moved toward a tripartite paper agreement. [evidence: 3]
Leasing flagged that the product name had changed across several drafts and requested a final confirmed name. [evidence: 7]
Leasing returned a signed contract scan; payment and shipment steps followed. [evidence: 9, 10]
Seller and leasing surfaced an unresolved inspection-versus-payment dependency: the lessor wanted photos/video, while the seller said final assembly depended on payment. [evidence: 11, 12]
Buyer confirmed funds had arrived but said its driver was waiting while the machine was not ready; buyer pressed for immediate shipment and offered to finish assembly itself. [evidence: 18]

primary_trajectory_explanation.category: Leasing/legal coordination followed by unresolved payment-to-readiness sequencing
primary_trajectory_explanation.explanation: The transaction progressed through legal revisions, signed documents, and leasing payment, but inspection requirements and client-specific completion were not aligned before shipment was arranged. At the last event, the buyer reported funds had arrived while the driver was waiting and the machine still needed work. This is the visible state of the process; later delivery or the final transaction result is not in the view. [evidence: 3, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 18]

secondary_factors: Buyer-side contact was busy and disputed that dimensions were missing; exact product data had to be recovered through another contact. [evidence: 2, 4]
Leasing's legal requirements drove the move to a tripartite paper contract and additional review. [evidence: 3, 5, 7]
The customer requested a rapid arrival by Wednesday and engaged transport before the seller had confirmed assembly and dispatch readiness. [evidence: 14, 15, 18]

what_could_be_done: Before signing, agree in writing on one final product name and a complete specification sheet across seller, lessee, and lessor. [evidence: 2, 4, 7]
Resolve the inspection/payment sequence with leasing before contract execution, including whether inspection can occur before client-specific assembly. [evidence: 11, 12]
Confirm assembly completion, payment receipt, loading time, carrier responsibilities, and acceptance location before the buyer dispatches a vehicle. [evidence: 14, 15, 16, 18]
limits: The lessor controls its legal review and payment release; the buyer controls its internal schedule and transport. [evidence: 3, 7, 11, 14]
The view ends during the shipment escalation; it does not show the callback, final readiness, or delivery. [evidence: 18]

evidence.paraphrase: Manager worklog says buyer wanted an in-stock capper/labeler, the approximate 3M price was acceptable, and the lead was not yet qualified.
Buyer said a prior supplier deal had gone badly and expected internal review to allow signing in the first half of the next week; exchanged a direct WhatsApp contact.
Buyer-side contact said she was too busy to fill the form and believed dimensions were already sent; manager said he would obtain exact data from the other contact.
Leasing contact and seller confirmed container dimensions and discussed a two-party versus three-party contract and which party would carry warranty obligations.
Seller legal and leasing discussed warranty terms and lessee identity; they agreed to prepare the tripartite paper-contract path for review.
Leasing requested the equipment conformity certificate or passport; the manager later said he requested it from production and sent the document.
Leasing said the equipment name had changed three times and requested written confirmation of the final name for the lease contract.
Leasing requested three signed paper copies be sent to the lessee and a scan returned.
Leasing sent a scan of the signed purchase contract.
Manager asked whether an invoice was required; leasing said payment would use the seller's existing bank details and that it was waiting for the customer's funds.
Manager worklog says leasing wanted equipment photos/video before paying, while the customer had paid the lessor; it says the lessor expected to transfer funds the next day.
Manager told leasing final assembly and client-specific labeling depended on funds; leasing said the customer had already paid and it was waiting on inspection before transferring money.
Leasing said it expected to send payment that day and asked about dispatch; manager said final assembly would follow receipt of funds.
Buyer-side contact asked the seller to arrange transport so the machine could arrive by Wednesday and requested a prompt callback with loading details.
Buyer asked for a firm next-day loading time and address; the manager said production timing was uncertain until payment arrived and the remaining work was confirmed.
Manager said the seller could not act as the buyer's delivery proxy and was waiting for production's dispatch timing.
Buyer said leasing had sent payment and a driver could come that day; manager said he was still checking whether funds had reached the seller.
Buyer confirmed funds had arrived about 20 minutes earlier, but its driver was waiting while the machine was not ready; buyer demanded prompt shipment and offered its technicians to finish the stand.

uncertainties: The approximate 3M price and initial in-stock status are recorded in a manager worklog, not directly confirmed by the buyer in these excerpts. [evidence: 0]
The view does not include the result of the promised callback, the final loading/delivery date, or the machine's completion. [evidence: 18]
The exact moment and amount of the buyer's down payment to the lessor are not shown in customer-sourced evidence; the manager worklog reports that it was paid. [evidence: 10]
